Content:
Suppose we want to compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x)] for the piecewise function [MATH: f(x)] given below.
[MATH: {x^{3}|forx < 1; 2|forx = 1; − (x − 1)^{3} + 3|forx > 1]

Content:
We begin by sketching a graph of the function:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ccc761bee442132a07fcdcca2dd26418]

Content:
To compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x),] we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

Content:
- Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x<1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x) = x^3.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{−})x^{3}; = 1^{3}; = 1.]
- Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=-(x-1)^3+3.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+}) − (x − 1)^{3} + 3; = − (1 − 1)^{3} + 3; = 3.]

Content:
Because the left and right-sided limits are not equal, the overall limit does not exist: [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x) = \text{DNE}.]

[MATH: f(x) = {4x^{3} − 2|forx < 1; 3x + b|forx > 1,]
it is known that [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)] exists. What is the value of the constant [MATH: b?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
In order for [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)] to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

  • Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x < 1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=4x^3-2.] We get [MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{−})4x^{3} − 2; = 4(1)^{3} − 2; = 2.]

  • Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)= 3x+b.] We get [MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})3x + b; = 3(1) + b; = 3 + b.]

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have [MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x); 2|= 3 + b; b|= − 1.]

- Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)= 3x+b.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})3x + b; = 3(1) + b; = 3 + b.]

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x); 2|= 3 + b; b|= − 1.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x)] for the piecewise function [MATH: f(x)] given below.
[MATH: {x^{3}|forx < 1; 2|forx = 1; − (x − 1)^{3} + 3|forx > 1]

Content:
We begin by sketching a graph of the function:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ccc761bee442132a07fcdcca2dd26418]

Content:
To compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x),] we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

Content:
- Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x<1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x) = x^3.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{−})x^{3}; = 1^{3}; = 1.]
- Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=-(x-1)^3+3.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+}) − (x − 1)^{3} + 3; = − (1 − 1)^{3} + 3; = 3.]

Content:
Because the left and right-sided limits are not equal, the overall limit does not exist: [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} f(x) = \text{DNE}.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing the One-Sided Limits of a Piecewise Function when the Limits Coincide

Example Prompt:
Find the left- and right-sided limits at [MATH: x=1] of the piecewise function [MATH: f(x)] defined by
[MATH: {6e^{x − 1}|forx < 1; x^{2} + 2x + 3|forx > 1.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x<1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x) = 6e^{x-1}.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{−})6e^{x − 1}; = 6e^{1 − 1}; = 6e^{0}; = 6.]

Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x) = x^2+2x+3.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})x^{2} + 2x + 3; = 1^{2} + 2(1) + 3; = 6.]

Item 5 — Example: Computing the One-Sided Limits of a Piecewise Function when the Limits Do Not Coincide

Find the left-sided and right-sided limits at [MATH: x=0] for the function

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x < 0,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=-x^2+3.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 0^{−})(− x^{2} + 3); = − (0)^{2} + 3; = 3.]

Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>0,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt{x}.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 0^{+})sqrt(x); = sqrt(0); = 0.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Limits of Piecewise Functions

Content:
Suppose we want to find [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)] for the piecewise function given by

Content:
[MATH: f(x) = {3^{x + 1}|forx < 0; sqrt(x^{2} + 9)|forx ≥ 0.]

Content:
To get an idea of the behavior of the function around [MATH: x=0,] we can plot the function.

Graphic:

Content:
To compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} f(x),] we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

Content:
- Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x < 0,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=3^{x+1}.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 0^{−})3^{x + 1}; = 3^{0 + 1}; = 3.]
- Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>0,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=\sqrt {x^2+9}.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 0^{+})sqrt(x^{2} + 9); = sqrt(0^{2} + 9); = 3.]

Content:
The left and right-sided limits both exist and are equal. So, the overall limit is

Content:
[MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 0} f(x) =3.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute [MATH: \lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} g(x),] we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

However, the right-sided limit [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1^+}g(x)] does not exist since [MATH: g(x)] is not defined in the interval [MATH: x\in(1,2).]

Consequently, the overall limit does not exist either:

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}g(x) = \text{DNE}.]

Item 12 — Example: Solving for a Constant Such that the Limit of a Piecewise Function Exists

Example Prompt:
For the piecewise function
[MATH: f(x) = {4x^{3} − 2|forx < 1; 3x + b|forx > 1,]
it is known that [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)] exists. What is the value of the constant [MATH: b?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In order for [MATH: \lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)] to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

- Approaching from the left, we have [MATH: x < 1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)=4x^3-2.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{−})4x^{3} − 2; = 4(1)^{3} − 2; = 2.]
- Approaching from the right, we have [MATH: x>1,] so we use the expression [MATH: f(x)= 3x+b.] We get
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})3x + b; = 3(1) + b; = 3 + b.]

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have
[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{−})f(x)|= lim_(x → 1^{+})f(x); 2|= 3 + b; b|= − 1.]
